Two drift over the white ceramic expanse like a miniature Siberia; one sits by itself on the windowsill; four make their way across the ceiling’s blank pale-yellow terrain; another works through the creases of a towel. Small bronze bodies, with antennae “strongly elbowed,” move across *Antony and Cleopatra*, which lies face down and unastonished; one lies dead in the raised ridge of a bar of soap. They belong to the subfamily Formicinae, marked by a single segment behind the thorax, their abdomens curved like crescent blades. One is caught among bubbles while I soak in the bath. They enter, apparently without aim, along the baseboard; they do not sting or bite, and under a fingertip they flatten without blood.

Peterson’s guide describes them as “social creatures,” but what a bleak community it is: look-alike wanderers, hard and seed-sized, stopping on their routes for only three seconds to touch faces with another. Some carry the dry, paper-thin bodies of the dead in their jaws, mandibles opening and shutting like the catch on a necklace. “Mating occurs in flight”—and really, what could be more fitting? A light, rash ecstasy: the winged queen and her partner whirl in a near-quantum ardor by the kumquat, after which she drops her wings and lays the pearl-colored larvae into sandy cradles. Then come more of those anvil-headed, creeping presences, tracing the cracks in the tile, the rim of the bathtub—and now one has begun crossing the mirror, doubled by its reflection.

The speaker notices countless tiny bronze ants wandering through the bathroom. They move across every surface: along the sill, over the ceiling, onto the towel and soap, into the tub, across the tile, and even over the mirror. Their presence is persistent and strangely aimless, as if the room has become a territory they are endlessly exploring.

These insects are identified as members of the Formicinae subfamily. They have the recognizable features of ants: elbowed antennae, waists made of a single segment, and curved, sickle-shaped abdomens. Their bodies are small and delicate, yet their movement gives them a steady, purposeful appearance, even when no clear purpose can be seen.

The ants seem to enter through the baseboard, emerging into the bathroom without any obvious goal. They do not bite or threaten the speaker, and they are easily crushed. When killed, they leave no blood behind, only tiny bodies. This makes them seem less like individual living beings and more like fragments of a larger, impersonal process.

Although ants are commonly described as social creatures, the society observed here appears grim, mechanical, and almost joyless. Their interactions are brief and minimal: they touch one another for a moment, then continue moving. Some carry the bodies of dead ants, suggesting a kind of communal behavior, but even this action feels automatic rather than tender or meaningful.

The text contrasts this ordinary, almost depressing scene of ants creeping through a bathroom with the far more dramatic image of their mating flight. In that moment, ants rise into the air, and reproduction becomes something grand and aerial. After mating, the queen sheds her wings and begins the work of producing a new generation. This contrast highlights the distance between the ants’ dull, mechanical wandering indoors and the extraordinary biological cycle that continues beyond it.
outputs.L4:
At first there were only three of them, or perhaps four, moving in a loose black punctuation across the white enamel of the bathroom sink. They appeared in the morning, when the room was still damp from the previous night’s shower and the mirror held a faint gray cloud at its edges. One ant stood near the chrome ring of the drain, its antennae touching and withdrawing from the metal as if testing a sealed door. Another crossed the tiled ledge beneath the toothbrush glass. A third made a brief, uncertain circuit around a drop of water and then bent its head to drink.

They were very small ants, not the large confident kind that enter a kitchen as if they have inherited it, but delicate, nearly weightless creatures, the size of crumbs. Their bodies were divided with the neatness of diagrams: head, thorax, abdomen; six legs jointed like tiny instruments; antennae moving constantly, feeling the world before the body committed itself. Under the harsh bathroom light they were not simply black but brown-black, with a faint shine, as though made of polished seed husk. They belonged, I supposed, to some common domestic species—one of the innumerable Formicidae that have accompanied human settlement for centuries, reading our walls and pipes as extensions of soil and root.

Their entrance was invisible. I searched for it along the baseboard, behind the sink pedestal, near the cracked seam where the bathtub met the floor. There was no obvious line of invasion, no procession like an illustration in a schoolbook. They arrived singly, almost shyly, emerging from gaps too small for the eye to honor as openings. The bathroom, which had seemed sealed and private, revealed itself as porous: a landscape of fissures, damp caverns, mineral cliffs, and reservoirs. To me it was a room of porcelain and towels. To them it was terrain.

For several days I watched before I interfered. Their movements had the appearance of purpose without the comfort of explanation. One ant would hurry along the grout between tiles, pause abruptly, turn back, touch another ant head to head, and then continue in a new direction. They seemed at once erratic and governed by laws. Their encounters were brief but charged: antenna to antenna, a flicker of information passing through bodies so small they could have been mistaken for dust. What was exchanged there? A map, an alarm, the location of moisture, the rumor of sugar, the chemical grammar of the colony? They did not speak, yet the whole species is a language of contact.

In the cabinet beneath the sink I found a few more, exploring the dark around the cleaning bottles. One had discovered the dried sweetness on the rim of a cough syrup cap and circled it with the devotion of a pilgrim. Another dragged a nearly invisible particle—soap, skin, plaster, food, who could say—back toward the wall. Its burden was larger than its head. It advanced by force of repetitions: pull, pause, adjust, pull again. There was something comic in the disproportion, and something heroic, though heroism is a dangerous word to apply to an insect. The ant did not choose difficulty as a human might, did not ennoble itself through effort. It simply continued.

Still, watching it, I felt the strange pressure of analogy. The bathroom was full of our own residues: hair in the drain, lint behind the door, fingerprints on the faucet, the evaporated salt of bathwater on the tile. We too leave trails, follow signals, divide labor, tend the young, remove the dead, build chambers around our needs. We too mistake our arrangements for permanence until some smaller life enters through the crack and proves how provisional the borders are.

After a week the infestation became less charming. There were ants in the bathtub and on the rim of the toilet tank. One wandered across the folded towel with an intimacy I resented. Another appeared near the toothpaste, and I imagined it vanishing into the bristles of my toothbrush, carrying on its feet the anonymous matter of pipes and walls. I wiped them away with a square of tissue. The gesture was easy, almost unconscious. A brief pressure of the thumb, and the intricate body became a dark smear.

This was the first death I noticed because I caused it. Others followed without my help. In the corner beside the bath mat, two ants lay curled like commas. On the windowsill, one had died on its back, legs drawn inward, a perfect emblem of collapse. Their dead did not look peaceful. They looked abandoned by the force that had made them legible. Alive, an ant is all direction; dead, it is only a fleck.

Yet even the dead entered the system. One morning I saw a living ant find the body of another near the baseboard. It paused, touched it, circled it, then gripped it and began to drag it away. The corpse snagged on a ridge of grout. The living ant reversed, pulled from another angle, disappeared behind the loosened edge of paint, and returned for the body again. I knew that many ants perform necrophoresis, carrying their dead from the nest in response to chemical signals released by decay. A corpse becomes, in that society, a message. Death has an odor; sanitation is a collective duty. What seemed to me like mourning was probably not mourning. But the distinction did not entirely comfort me. Our own rituals are also made of instinct, training, fear, and chemistry. We dignify the removal of the dead because we can name it.

There must have been a queen somewhere beyond the wall, though I never saw her. Hidden in a chamber of damp wood or soil, she would have been the still center of this activity, a body devoted to reproduction, fed and groomed by workers whose individual lives were brief and functional. The ants in my bathroom were likely sterile females, sisters in a vast household organized not by affection as we understand it but by kinship, pheromone, and necessity. Their private selves, if they had such a thing, were subordinate to the colony’s persistence. Each one seemed solitary when I saw it crossing the sink, yet none existed alone. The smallest ant carried an invisible multitude with it.

This was what made them alien: not their bodies, though those were alien enough, with their armored segments and trembling antennae, but their way of being a self only partially. An ant is an individual and also an extension of a larger organism, a cell wandering at a distance from the body to which it belongs. The colony thinks without a brain, remembers without a single memory, chooses without a central will. It is difficult not to envy this, and difficult not to fear it. Human life is crowded with loneliness. Ant life, from the outside, appears crowded with purpose.

I tried the usual remedies. I cleaned the sink with vinegar. I sealed a crack with white caulk, badly. I moved the wastebasket and rinsed the medicine caps. For a day the ants disappeared, and the bathroom regained its illusion of emptiness. Then one returned, moving along the tub as if tracing the edge of a continent. It stopped at the place where the caulk had dried and touched it with its antennae. The old passage was closed. The ant turned, explored the perimeter, and eventually found another route behind the radiator pipe.

This persistence was irritating and admirable in equal measure. They did not rage at obstruction or despair at loss. They recalculated. Their lives were made of interruption. A drop of water was a lake, a human foot a catastrophe, a line of disinfectant an invisible wall of poison and scent. Still they went on, because going on was not a decision but the structure of their existence. To live, for them, was to search; to find, to report; to die, to be removed; to hatch, to replace.

One afternoon I noticed several winged ants near the window, larger than the others, restless in the light. Alates, I thought: reproductive males or virgin queens, produced when the colony had accumulated enough strength to risk expansion. They climbed the glass and fell back, climbed and fell, drawn toward the pale square of sky they could not reach. In another setting they might have flown out in a nuptial swarm, mating in the air, founding new colonies in soil or rot. Here, in the bathroom, their wings were absurd and tragic, delicate transparencies beating against a closed window. Reproduction, that grand biological promise, had become a confused flutter between the toothbrush cup and the sill.

I opened the window. A few escaped; others did not understand the opening. One remained on the frame for a long time, its wings catching the light like scraps of cellophane. I wanted it to leave, but I also wanted to see what it would do. At last a draft lifted it, or it lifted itself, and it vanished outward into the day with no more ceremony than a speck of ash.

The infestation dwindled after that. Whether because of my cleaning, the changing weather, or some internal decision of the colony, fewer ants appeared. The bathroom settled back into its ordinary scale. The sink was a sink again, not a basin rimmed by explorers. The tile was tile, not a plain crossed by black travelers. Yet for a while I continued to look for them. I would pause before turning on the tap, scanning the porcelain for movement. Absence itself became a kind of afterimage.

What had they been, finally? A nuisance, certainly. A hygiene problem. An incursion. But also a revelation of the unnoticed life that presses against our own from every side. Their smallness did not make them simple. Within each ant was a machinery of appetite and response; beyond each ant, a society older than ours, more durable in many ways, indifferent to our categories of home and trespass. They entered through the cracks because cracks exist. They drank from our droplets because water gathers there. They died under our fingers because we are large and careless. They continued because life, at its most basic, is continuation.

I do not want ants in the bathroom. This remains true. But I cannot quite return them to the status of mere pests. I have seen one carry a dead sister away. I have seen one drink from a bead of water as though from a well. I have watched a winged ant fling itself at a window, bearing in its fragile body the future of an unseen kingdom. Their world is not gentle, and neither is ours. Yet in their blind, minute persistence there is a kind of severity that resembles wisdom: build, search, touch, carry, vanish; and somewhere behind the wall, begin again.
outputs.L5:
Two travelers crossed the vast silence of Siberia, where the snow stretched endlessly beneath a pale winter sky. One was a young cartographer, eager to draw the forgotten edges of the world; the other was Antony, an old storyteller who claimed that every river, forest, and mountain carried a memory.

As they journeyed through frozen valleys and past villages warmed by firelight, Antony spoke of courage, patience, and the strange beauty of lonely places. The young traveler listened, realizing that Siberia was not empty at all. It was filled with hidden life: the tracks of wolves, the whisper of pine trees, and the quiet strength of people who called the harsh land home.

By the time the two reached the edge of a great frozen lake, the cartographer understood that maps could show distance, but only stories could reveal meaning. And in Siberia, Antony’s stories made the cold world feel alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about observing ants in a bathroom, blending precise entomological details with domestic imagery and a slightly dark, philosophical tone.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn they appear on the bathroom tile as if summoned by a hairline crack in the world: a black seam come unstitched, bead by bead, across the porcelain continent.

They are small enough to be mistaken for punctuation. Yet each is complete: six jointed legs ticking beneath a chitinous gloss, elbowed antennae tasting the air where I left the ghost of toothpaste, mandibles opening and closing with the patient seriousness of tools. Their waists are cinched into narrow petioles, delicate as if made by a jeweler with morbid interests. Head, thorax, abdomen—three thoughts of one body—moving through the blue morning light reflected from the sink.

They travel along the baseboard in a procession of obedience, laying and reading their invisible scripture of pheromones. One turns aside to examine a drop of water trembling near the drain, a planet with a silver skin. Another circles the fallen eyelash I shed in the night, measuring the relic of a giant. Around the toilet’s porcelain foot they gather like pilgrims at a white ruin. The bathmat, damp and frayed, becomes a savanna. The grout lines are roads. The cabinet’s shadow is weather.

I stand barefoot above them, enormous and ashamed, holding a towel like a flag of surrender. The mirror keeps my face in its cold rectangle; behind me the shower curtain hangs, pale and limp, like a sail from a wrecked ship. Soap dries in its dish. A razor rusts by degrees. The room smells faintly of lavender, bleach, skin, and the mineral breath of pipes. All my arrangements—comb, cup, folded washcloth, the bright medicine bottles promising relief—seem suddenly ceremonial, provisional, no more enduring than the sugar fleck they have found beneath the sink.

How confidently they enter the architecture of my privacy. They do not know privacy. They know gradients, hunger, colony, trail. Somewhere behind the wall a queen pulses in the dark, swollen with futures, while workers pass through the cracks carrying news in their bodies. They are not lost. I am the lost thing, towering in a tiled chamber built for washing away evidence.

One ant climbs the slick cliff of the bathtub and fails, slips, climbs again. Its legs adhere, release, adhere, each tarsal pad negotiating with the impossible smoothness. There is no drama in its struggle, no appeal. It is only life applying itself to matter. Watching it, I feel the small hinge of pity open and close inside me.

Then I turn on the faucet.

The water comes first as a cough, then as a clear, municipal thunder. The ants nearest the sink scatter, their antennae frantic apostrophes. A few are taken instantly, swept into the chrome mouth of the drain, where darkness accepts them without philosophy. Others survive by accident, clinging to a ridge of caulk, trembling with a kind of minute electricity.

I tell myself I am only keeping house. I tell myself boundaries matter. I tell myself the dead are uncountable and therefore absolved from accusation.

Still, all day, the bathroom keeps their lesson. In the white basin, one drowned body remains caught against a crescent of soap scum: lacquered head, folded legs, abdomen shining like a seed. By evening even that will be gone, rinsed away by teeth-brushing, hand-washing, the ordinary liturgies of cleanliness.

But beneath the floor, in the damp arithmetic of the walls, the colony continues—blind, chemical, immaculate. And I, too, continue: mammal, tenant, temporary weather; lifting the lid, washing my hands, stepping carefully over the place where a dark line once wrote itself across the tile and asked, without words, what separates a home from a grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, literary paragraph in the style of a naturalist’s notebook turned surreal meditation, describing tiny bronze ants crawling around a bathtub and bathroom.
counterfactuals.output: At the porcelain escarpment of the bathtub, where a crescent of dried soap had hardened into a pale mineral deposit, the ants appeared at dusk: minute bronze articulations, each no larger than a moving comma, filing from the cracked grout with the grave industry of surveyors sent ahead of a vanished empire. They explored the enamel basin as if it were a salt-white valley scoured by ancient floods, pausing at hairs curled like blackened reeds, at droplets trembling in the chrome’s cold moons, at the tub drain’s dark oculus where the world seemed to inhale. In the bathroom’s damp republic they found continents in every surface—the bathmat a matted savanna, the sink a cliff of glazed limestone, the mirror a vertical pond in which no ant was reflected, only the enormous ghost of the observer leaning in, notebook useless, breath clouding the glass like weather. Their bodies caught the light with a faint metallic fever, bronze not as statues are bronze but as buried seeds, as coins tongued smooth by the dead; and watching them thread the rim of the tub, vanish beneath the shampoo bottle, return from behind the toilet with inscrutable tidings, I felt the room loosen from its domestic name and become a cavern, a shrine, a skull washed clean and inhabited by thoughts too small to kill.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem that begins by counting ants in different places—windowsill, ceiling, towel, soap—and gradually expands into reflections on ant society, mating, death, and reproduction.
counterfactuals.output:
One ant on the windowsill, black comma in the morning light. Two ants on the ceiling, moving as if gravity were only a rumor they had agreed not to repeat. Three ants on the towel, lost in the white terry fields, climbing the loops like hills. Four ants on the soap, circling the oval moon of it, tasting lavender, salt, the faint human weather left behind by hands.

Then more: a thin punctuation along the baseboard, a nervous scripture under the sink, a congregation in the crack where the tile has opened its mouth. I begin by counting and fail almost immediately. Ants are an argument against the single life. Each one is small enough to be overlooked, yet together they revise the room. They make a map of my neglect. They find the sugar sealed inside its paper cathedral, the crumb under the table, the drop I did not know I spilled.

What do they say to one another with their bodies? Here is hunger. Here is danger. Here is the way. They touch and are informed. They vanish and are continued. No ant is lonely in the way I understand loneliness, no ant is private in the way I have made privacy into a room with a locked door and a name on the mail. Their society is a dark intelligence distributed among legs, jaws, antennae, a thought that does not need a thinker, a city carried in thousands of brief, obedient sparks.

Some are born to labor, and labor until their little machinery stops. Some are born with wings, with the terrible luxury of flight. Once, after rain, the air fills with them: males and queens rising from hidden chambers, sudden saints of the underground, lifting themselves into the bright, indifferent afternoon. They mate in midair, as if love were an accident of weather, as if the future required only collision, release, a fall back to earth. The males die soon after, emptied of their errand. The queens tear off their own wings, those delicate permissions, and go down into darkness to begin again.

There, in the sealed chamber, she becomes an engine of continuance. Egg after egg, the pale grammar of survival. Daughters hatch to feed her, clean her, carry the blind white larvae like ideas not yet hardened into shape. The dead are removed. The tunnels lengthen. The colony remembers without memorials. It does not weep, but it wastes nothing—not the body, not the path, not the message laid down in scent and fading.

I am still standing in the bathroom with the towel in my hand, watching one ant struggle over the slick blue cliff of soap. I could drown it with a thumbful of water. I could spare it. Mercy, too, is a kind of accident at this scale. Around us, the house goes on pretending it is mine. Beneath us, behind us, inside the walls, another nation touches its way through the dark, bearing crumbs, bearing eggs, bearing its dead, endless and exact, devoted not to meaning but to more life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ornate, image-rich piece about a minor ant infestation in a bathroom, incorporating phrases like “strongly elbowed,” “Sub-family Formicinae,” and “mating occurs in flight.”
counterfactuals.output:
At first it was only a punctuation of blackness on the porcelain: one ant, then another, then a wavering semicolon procession along the rim of the bathtub, each body lacquered and minute, each leg moving with the delicate certainty of calligraphy. The bathroom, usually a kingdom of steam and tile, had become a marshland of rumor. They emerged from the hairline shadow behind the sink, from that narrow, damp border where the wall surrendered to the baseboard, as if the house itself had begun writing in insects.

They were not many—nothing biblical, nothing to send one fleeing with a towel clutched to the breast—but their smallness gave them a certain sinister refinement. A minor ant infestation is still an invasion when it occurs beside the toothbrush cup. Their antennae, strongly elbowed, flicked and questioned the world: the fallen crystal of toothpaste, the sweet ghost of hand soap, the damp crescent beneath the soap dish. They investigated the chrome faucet with priestly diligence, their dark bodies reflected and multiplied in the gleam until six ants became sixty in the trembling mirror of metal.

I imagined them as aristocrats of some hidden province, envoys of the Sub-family Formicinae, wearing their segmented armor like mourning clothes. Their waists were cinched as if by invisible corsets; their abdomens shone like drops of burnt sugar. They moved with a confidence that seemed wildly disproportionate to their size, scaling the cliff face of a shampoo bottle, crossing the white tundra of the sink basin, vanishing and returning through a crack no wider than a line of ink.

Outside, perhaps, their grander dramas unfolded beneath stones and roots: queens in subterranean chambers, larvae like grains of rice, the old green world humming above them. Somewhere in that vast ant mythology, mating occurs in flight—an airy and perilous ceremony, love lifted briefly into the sky before wings are shed and kingdoms are founded in darkness. But here, in the bathroom, their epic had narrowed to a damp smear near the drain, a sugared residue, a map of scent invisible to human eyes.

I wiped the counter. The procession broke, scattered, re-formed. One ant stood alone on the edge of the tub, poised against the glossy abyss, heroic as a traveler at the end of the known world. Then it turned, antennae trembling, and hurried back toward the secret gate behind the sink, carrying with it news of bleach, giants, and the pale moon of the bathroom light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Nabokov-like descriptive passage where someone soaking in a tub notices ants moving over books, soap, tiles, and a mirror, mixing scientific observation with sensual metaphor.
counterfactuals.output:
In the tepid amphitheater of the tub, where my knees rose like two pale islands through a satin archipelago of suds, I first observed the ants.

They had come in a black, thinking seam from the crack beneath the window, each one a lacquered comma, an articulated doubt, a tiny machine carrying its own night. They advanced over the books I had stacked, with criminal optimism, upon the wicker stool: across a damp-spotted volume of poems, over the swollen blue boards of a field guide, along the gilt edge of a novel whose pages had curled in the steam like leaves held over a flame. One ant paused upon the printed word *nectar*, palpating it with the tremulous tips of her antennae, as though reading not by sight but by thirst.

Their order was not order, precisely, but a congress of corrections. A scout, finding the fragrant cliff of soap, turned back; another mounted it and slid, fantastically, down the green oval slope, leaving no trace upon its glycerin moon. Around the porcelain dish they circled with the fervor of astronomers who have mistaken a planet for a fruit. On the tiles, where beads of bathwater shone in the grout, they bent to drink from each convex world, magnified there for an instant: head, thorax, abdomen—three polished syllables of appetite.

I, meanwhile, lay immersed, my skin loosened into luxury, my toes dim and pink beneath the water’s opaline blur. The scent of almond soap, wet paper, and my own heated flesh mingled in the small room. Above me the mirror, fogged to a milky cataract, received their expedition in ghostly duplicate. The ants crossed its lower edge in procession, and in that blurred silver their bodies became eyelashes, musical notes, stitches sewing the bathroom to some darker outdoors.

One reached the mirror’s center and touched its reflection. For a moment she conversed with her impossible twin—antenna to antenna, desire to desire—then turned away, briskly persuaded by whatever chemistry rules the miniature republics of hunger. I watched, deliciously helpless, while the bath cooled around me and the books drank steam, and the ants went on translating the room into trails: sugarless, tireless, intimate as a thought moving over the body before sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
